slides.visual_description: The Economic & Structural Reality — Explain how rising national health expenditures and the shift from independent practice to employment within large health systems change physician autonomy and make enterprise navigation necessary.
slides.narration_text: To set the stage, look to the left: the upward line labeled “National Health Expenditures … $5.2 Trillion” isn’t just a big number—it signals that healthcare now behaves like a macroeconomic force that shapes how every decision is financed and scrutinized. On the right, the paired bars showing independent practice shrinking while hospital employment grows tell the second half of the story—care is delivered inside large enterprises where governance, scale, and standardization redefine day-to-day autonomy. The implication is practical: impact now depends on learning to navigate—and influence—the enterprise, not just optimizing a single clinic.
slides.script_notes: The Economic & Structural Reality — Explain how rising national health expenditures and the shift from independent practice to employment within large health systems change physician autonomy and make enterprise navigation necessary.

slides.display_title: The Human Cost: System Waste & Burnout
slides.visual_description: The Human Cost: System Waste & Burnout — Interpret administrative waste and physician burnout as linked system-design problems rather than isolated individual resilience issues.
slides.narration_text: Notice how the left statistic—about a quarter of spending tied to administrative waste—pairs with the right-side burnout figure to reveal cause and consequence inside the same system. That burnout badge isn’t about patient volume; it reflects the daily drag of bureaucratic tasks that siphon time and attention from care. Read together, these visuals reframe burnout from an individual resilience issue to a design flaw—precisely the kind of friction where redesign and process simplification can return time to patients and meaning to work.
slides.script_notes: The Human Cost: System Waste & Burnout — Interpret administrative waste and physician burnout as linked system-design problems rather than isolated individual resilience issues.

slides.visual_description: The Knowledge Explosion & New Technologies — Describe how rapid medical knowledge growth, expanding AI use, remote monitoring, and VR training create both opportunity and the need for safe clinical oversight.
slides.narration_text: Follow the timeline: from the 1950 marker to today’s 73-day doubling, the compression of medical knowledge outpaces any static curriculum, so competence now includes how we oversee tools. Midway, the AI usage icon—two-thirds of physicians—underscores that oversight isn’t optional. And the remote-monitoring and VR callouts point to the upside: programs that shift COPD and heart failure care from reactive to proactive, and simulations that let teams rehearse without risk. The opportunity is real, but it’s safe only when clinicians set the guardrails and validate the workflows.
slides.script_notes: The Knowledge Explosion & New Technologies — Describe how rapid medical knowledge growth, expanding AI use, remote monitoring, and VR training create both opportunity and the need for safe clinical oversight.

slides.display_title: The Consumer Shift & The Digital Front Door
slides.visual_description: The Consumer Shift & The Digital Front Door — Explain how changing patient expectations for transparency, access, and convenience require intentional design of a frictionless digital care journey.
slides.narration_text: Start at the smartphone entry point and trace the journey to the provider icon: where the AI-driven triage node sits is where abandonment or acceleration happens. Jefferson Health’s example on screen illustrates the difference between a portal and a true front door—identity, triage, scheduling, and messaging stitched into one flow so patients move without handoffs. The design goal is simple to say and hard to build: make every digital step feel inevitable, so clinical steps can be intentional.
slides.script_notes: The Consumer Shift & The Digital Front Door — Explain how changing patient expectations for transparency, access, and convenience require intentional design of a frictionless digital care journey.

slides.visual_description: The Leadership Gap — Identify the mismatch between physicians’ interest in leadership and the limited formal executive training available, and explain why clinicians must bridge practice, business, and technology strategy.
slides.narration_text: Compare the bars: the tall column for physicians interested in leadership versus the much shorter one for formal executive training reveals a readiness–preparation gap. That gap explains stalled initiatives inside Academic Health Centers—clinical expertise is abundant, but incentives and cross-disciplinary fluency are thin. The path forward is clear: clinicians who can translate bedside insight into operational, business, and technology strategy will move systems faster and safer.
slides.script_notes: The Leadership Gap — Identify the mismatch between physicians’ interest in leadership and the limited formal executive training available, and explain why clinicians must bridge practice, business, and technology strategy.

slides.visual_description: Part 2 Summary & Knowledge Check — Synthesize the structural, human, technological, consumer, and leadership drivers into a single case for deliberate clinician leadership in shaping the future of care.
slides.narration_text: As we close, read the bullets as one arc: structural pressure and consolidation, human cost from waste and burnout, accelerating knowledge with new tools, and consumer expectations for seamless access—all converging on a leadership gap. The bold line at the bottom makes the ask explicit: translate clinical expertise into deliberate system leadership so technology and process actually improve outcomes and clinician well-being.
slides.script_notes: Part 2 Summary & Knowledge Check — Synthesize the structural, human, technological, consumer, and leadership drivers into a single case for deliberate clinician leadership in shaping the future of care.
